title.raw: 卷一百〇三 表第四 諸王世表四 Volume 103 Tables 4: Princes 4

sentences.zh: 建文初，封弟允熥爲吳王，允熞爲衡王，允熙爲徐王，皆懿文太子子也。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Jianwen, his younger brothers Yun Ting were enfeoffed as Prince of Wu, Yun Chi as Prince of Heng, and Yun Xi as Prince of Xu — all sons of the Crown Prince Yi Wen.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Jianwen reign, the emperor enfeoffed his younger brothers Yun Ting as Prince of Wu, Yun Chi as Prince of Heng, and Yun Xi as Prince of Xu; all were sons of the Crown Prince Yi Wen.

sentences.zh: 福王時，追諡吳王曰悼，衡王曰愍，徐王曰哀，見福王傳。

translations.literal: During the time of the Prince of Fu, posthumous titles were granted: the Prince of Wu was titled Dao, the Prince of Heng Min, and the Prince of Xu Ai — see the biography of the Prince of Fu.
translations.idiomatic: Under the Prince of Fu, posthumous titles were conferred on the Prince of Wu as Dao, the Prince of Heng as Min, and the Prince of Xu as Ai; see the biography of the Prince of Fu.

sentences.zh: 吳 悼王允熥，懿文太子嫡三子，建文元年封，未就藩。成祖入京師，降封廣澤王，居漳州。其年九月召還，廢爲庶人。永樂十五年卒。

translations.literal: Wu — Prince Dao Yun Ting, the third legitimate son of the Crown Prince Yi Wen, was enfeoffed in the first year of Jianwen and did not go to his fief. When Chengzu entered the capital, he was demoted to Prince of Guangze and lived at Zhangzhou. That year in the ninth month he was recalled and degraded to commoner status. He died in the fifteenth year of Yongle.
translations.idiomatic: Wu princedom — Prince Dao Yun Ting, the Crown Prince Yi Wen's third legitimate son, was enfeoffed in Jianwen 1 but never took up his fief. After Chengzu entered the capital, he was demoted to Prince of Guangze and lodged at Zhangzhou; recalled that ninth month and reduced to a commoner. He died in Yongle year 15.

cells.content: 衡 愍王允熞，懿文太子庶四子，建文元年封，未就藩。成祖入京師，降封懷恩王，居建昌。其年，與吳王俱召還，廢爲庶人。

translations.literal: Heng — Prince Min Yun Chi, the fourth son by a concubine of the Crown Prince Yi Wen, was enfeoffed in the first year of Jianwen and did not go to his fief. When Chengzu entered the capital, he was demoted to Prince of Huai'en and lived at Jianchang. That year, together with the Prince of Wu, he was recalled and degraded to commoner status.
translations.idiomatic: Heng princedom — Prince Min Yun Chi, the Crown Prince Yi Wen's fourth son by a secondary consort, was enfeoffed in Jianwen 1 but never went to his fief. After Chengzu took the capital he was demoted to Prince of Huai'en at Jianchang; that same year he and the Prince of Wu were recalled and stripped to commoner rank.

cells.content: 徐 哀簡王允熙，懿文太子庶五子，建文元年封，未就藩。成祖入京師，降封敷惠王，隨母居太子陵。永樂二年改封甌寧王，奉懿文祀。四年卒。無子，除。

translations.literal: Xu — Prince Ai Jian Yun Xi, the fifth son by a concubine of the Crown Prince Yi Wen, was enfeoffed in the first year of Jianwen and did not go to his fief. When Chengzu entered the capital, he was demoted to Prince of Fuhui and lived with his mother at the crown prince's tomb. In the second year of Yongle he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Ouning to maintain the sacrifices to Yi Wen. He died in the fourth year. He had no sons; the line was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Xu princedom — Prince Ai Jian Yun Xi, the Crown Prince Yi Wen's fifth son by a concubine, was enfeoffed in Jianwen 1 but never took his fief. After Chengzu entered the capital he was demoted to Prince of Fuhui and dwelt with his mother at the crown prince's mausoleum; in Yongle year 2 he was made Prince of Ouning to tend Yi Wen's cult. He died in year 4 without heirs, and the line was extinguished.

translations.literal: Chengzu had four sons.
translations.idiomatic: Chengzu had four sons.

translations.literal: Apart from the future Renzong, Gao Xi was not enfeoffed.
translations.idiomatic: Aside from the future Renzong, Gao Xi received no princely enfeoffment.

sentences.zh: 其得封者二王，曰漢王高煦，曰趙簡王高燧。

translations.literal: Of those who received enfeoffment there were two princes: Prince of Han Gao Xu and Prince Jian of Zhao Gao Sui.
translations.idiomatic: Two sons were enfeoffed: Gao Xu as Prince of Han and Gao Sui as Prince Jian of Zhao.

sentences.zh: 漢 高煦，成祖嫡二子。洪武二十八年封高陽王，永樂二年進封。十五年就藩樂安州。宣德元年八月反，削爵錮西內，焚死。世子瞻坦先卒。韋妃及九子俱從死，除。

translations.literal: Han — Gao Xu, the second legitimate son of Chengzu, was enfeoffed as Prince of Gaoyang in the twenty-eighth year of Hongwu and advanced in enfeoffment in the second year of Yongle. In the fifteenth year he went to his fief at Le'an. In the eighth month of the first year of Xuande he rebelled; his title was stripped, he was imprisoned in the western inner quarters, and burned to death. His heir Zhan Tan had died earlier. Consort Wei and nine sons all died with him; the line was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Han princedom — Gao Xu, Chengzu's second legitimate son, was made Prince of Gaoyang in Hongwu year 28, promoted in Yongle year 2, and took up his fief at Le'an in year 15. He rebelled in the eighth month of Xuande year 1, was stripped of rank, confined in the western palace, and burned to death. His heir Zhan Tan had predeceased him; Consort Wei and nine sons perished with him, and the line ended.

cells.content: 趙 簡王高燧，成祖嫡三子，永樂二年封。洪熙元年就藩彰德府。宣德六年薨。世子瞻坺先卒。

translations.literal: Zhao — Prince Jian Gao Sui, the third legitimate son of Chengzu, was enfeoffed in the second year of Yongle. In the first year of Hongxi he went to his fief at Zhangde Prefecture. He died in the sixth year of Xuande. His heir Zhan Fu had died earlier.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao princedom — Prince Jian Gao Sui, Chengzu's third legitimate son, was enfeoffed in Yongle year 2, took up his fief at Zhangde in Hongxi 1, and died in Xuande year 6. His heir Zhan Fu had predeceased him.

cells.content: 惠王瞻塙，簡嫡二子，初封安陽王，宣德七年襲封。景泰五年薨。

translations.literal: Prince Hui Zhan Tang, the second legitimate son of Prince Jian, was first enfeoffed as Prince of Anyang and succeeded to the enfeoffment in the seventh year of Xuande. He died in the fifth year of Jingtai.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Hui (Zhan Tang), Prince Jian's second legitimate son, was first made Prince of Anyang, inherited the Zhao line in Xuande year 7, and died in Jingtai year 5.

translations.literal: Prince Dao Qi Jin, the first legitimate son of Prince Hui, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the sixth year of Jingtai. He died in the fourth year of Tianshun.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Dao (Qi Jin), Prince Hui's first legitimate son, inherited the title in Jingtai year 6 and died in Tianshun year 4.

translations.idiomatic: Prince Jing (Jian Yao), Prince Dao's first son by a concubine, inherited in Chenghua 1 and died in Hongzhi year 15.

translations.literal: Prince Zhuang You Li, the third son by a concubine of Prince Jing, was first enfeoffed as Prince of Qingliu and succeeded to the enfeoffment in the sixteenth year of Hongzhi. He died in the thirteenth year of Zhengde.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Zhuang (You Li), Prince Jing's third son by a concubine, was first Prince of Qingliu, succeeded in Hongzhi year 16, and died in Zhengde year 13.

translations.literal: Prince Kang Hou Yu, the first legitimate son of Prince Zhuang, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the sixteenth year of Zhengde. He died in the thirty-ninth year of Jiajing.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Kang (Hou Yu), Prince Zhuang's first legitimate son, inherited in Zhengde year 16 and died in Jiajing year 39.

cells.content: 載培，康庶一子，初封獲嘉王。嘉靖十六年薨，諡昭定。後以孫常清襲趙封，進封親王，改諡曰恭。

translations.literal: Zai Pei, the first son by a concubine of Prince Kang, was first enfeoffed as Prince of Huojia. He died in the sixteenth year of Jiajing and was posthumously titled Zhao Ding. Later, because his grandson Chang Qing succeeded to the Zhao enfeoffment, he was advanced to prince of the first rank and his posthumous title was changed to Gong.

translations.literal: Yi Qian, the first legitimate son of Prince Gong, was enfeoffed as heir apparent in the twenty-eighth year of Jiajing. He died in the thirty-eighth year. His son Chang Qing succeeded to the enfeoffment. He was posthumously enfeoffed as prince with the posthumous title An.

translations.idiomatic: Prince Ci 𢣴, the Prince of Shouguang's first legitimate son You Gui, was redesignated heir apparent in the Wanli period and succeeded to the Zhao line in year 45.

translations.literal: Prince Ronghe Jian Zhi, the first legitimate son of Prince Gong'an, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the twenty-third year of Chenghua. He died in the eleventh year of Zhengde.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Ronghe (Jian Zhi), Prince Gong'an's first legitimate son, inherited in Chenghua year 23 and died in Zhengde year 11.

translations.literal: You Yi, the first son by a concubine of Prince Ronghe, was enfeoffed as Defender-General of the State in the twenty-third year of Chenghua. sentences.zh: 簡王祁鍈，靖嫡一子，成化四年襲封。弘治八年薨。

translations.literal: Prince Jian Qi Yin, the first legitimate son of Prince Jing, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the fourth year of Chenghua. He died in the eighth year of Hongzhi.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Jian (Qi Yin), Prince Jing's first legitimate son, inherited in Chenghua year 4 and died in Hongzhi year 8.

sentences.zh: 見滋，簡嫡一子，成化七年封世子。十五年薨。以子祐枔襲封。追封王，諡曰僖。

translations.literal: Jian Zi, the first legitimate son of Prince Jian, was enfeoffed as heir apparent in the seventh year of Chenghua. He died in the fifteenth year. Because his son You Xin succeeded to the enfeoffment, he was posthumously enfeoffed as prince with the posthumous title Xi.
translations.idiomatic: Jian Zi, Prince Jian's first legitimate son, was named heir apparent in Chenghua year 7 and died in year 15; his son You Xin's succession brought him a posthumous princedom as Prince Xi.

sentences.zh: 康王祐枔，僖嫡一子，弘治十四年襲封。正德二年薨。無子，從弟祐檡立。 懿王祐檡，東垣端惠王嫡一子，初襲東垣王，正德四年嗣封。十六年薨。

translations.literal: Prince Kang You Xin, the first legitimate son of Prince Xi, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the fourteenth year of Hongzhi. He died in the second year of Zhengde. He had no sons; his younger cousin You Ji was established. Prince Yi You Ji, the first legitimate son of Prince Duan Hui of Dongyuan, had first succeeded as Prince of Dongyuan and in the fourth year of Zhengde succeeded to the main line. He died in the sixteenth year.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Kang (You Xin), Prince Xi's first legitimate son, inherited in Hongzhi year 14 and died in Zhengde year 2 without heirs; his younger cousin You Ji took the line. Prince Yi (You Ji), the Prince of Dongyuan Duan Hui's first legitimate son, had first held Dongyuan and succeeded to Zheng in Zhengde year 4, dying in year 16.

sentences.zh: 恭王厚烷，懿嫡四子，嘉靖六年襲封。二十九年以諫帝真修，降庶人，發高牆。隆慶元年復爵，加祿四百石。萬曆十九年薨。

translations.literal: Prince Gong Hou Wan, the fourth legitimate son of Prince Yi, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the sixth year of Jiajing. In the twenty-ninth year, for remonstrating against the emperor's pursuit of true cultivation, he was degraded to commoner status and sent to the high wall. In the first year of Longqing his title was restored and four hundred piculs of stipend were added. He died in the nineteenth year of Wanli.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Gong (Hou Wan), Prince Yi's fourth legitimate son, inherited in Jiajing year 6. In year 29 he was reduced to a commoner and confined in the high wall for opposing the emperor's Daoist cultivation; Longqing year 1 restored his rank with four hundred additional piculs of stipend. He died in Wanli year 19.

sentences.zh: 端清世子載堉，恭嫡一子，嘉靖二十五年封世子。萬曆三十三年讓爵載壐。詔載堉及子翊錫，准以世子、世孫祿終身。其子孫仍封東垣王，以接見𣹟之統。 王載壐，恭再從弟庶人厚煒嫡一子，盟津王見濍曾孫也。以載堉讓爵，萬曆三十四年受封，薨。

translations.literal: Heir apparent Duan Qing Zai Ji, the first legitimate son of Prince Gong, was enfeoffed as heir apparent in the twenty-fifth year of Jiajing. In the thirty-third year of Wanli he yielded the title to Zai Qian. An edict granted Zai Ji and his son Yi Xi stipends as heir apparent and heir apparent's son for life. His descendants were still enfeoffed as princes of Dongyuan to continue the line of Jian 𣹟. Prince Zai Qian, the first legitimate son of the commoner Hou Wei, who was the second cousin once removed of Prince Gong, was the great-great-grandson of Prince of Mengjin Jian Yin. Because Zai Ji yielded the title, he received enfeoffment in the thirty-fourth year of Wanli and died.
translations.idiomatic: Heir apparent Duan Qing (Zai Ji), Prince Gong's first legitimate son, was named heir in Jiajing year 25 and in Wanli year 33 ceded the succession to Zai Qian; an edict allowed Zai Ji and his son Yi Xi lifetime stipends as heir and heir's son while their line continued as princes of Dongyuan to preserve Jian 𣹟's descent. Prince Zai Qian, the legitimate son of the disgraced Hou Wei (Prince Gong's second cousin once removed) and great-great-grandson of the Prince of Mengjin Jian Yin, took the title when Zai Ji yielded it in Wanli year 34 and died.

sentences.zh: 王翊鐘，載壐嫡一子，萬曆三十五年封世子，既而襲封。崇禎十三年以罪賜死，除。

translations.literal: Prince Yi Zhong, the first legitimate son of Zai Qian, was enfeoffed as heir apparent in the thirty-fifth year of Wanli and soon afterward succeeded to the enfeoffment. In the thirteenth year of Chongzhen he was sentenced to death for a crime; the line was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Prince Yi Zhong, Zai Qian's first legitimate son, was named heir in Wanli year 35, inherited shortly thereafter, and was ordered to die for his crimes in Chongzhen year 13; the main Zheng line ended.

translations.literal: Prince Chang 𰜴, the first legitimate son of Prince Gong Yi, was re-enfeoffed as eldest son from the rank of Defender-General of the State in the twenty-fifth year of Wanli. In the thirty-seventh year he succeeded to the enfeoffment. He died in the forty-second year. Prince Chang Jie, the first legitimate son of Yi Tai, second son of heir apparent Duan Qing, was first enfeoffed as Bulwark-General of the State; by an edict during the Wanli reign he was still enfeoffed as Prince of Dongyuan. In the eighth year of Chongzhen, when the Prince of Dongyuan You Bin died, he succeeded to the enfeoffment.

translations.literal: Jian Xiao, the first legitimate son of Prince Jing, succeeded to the enfeoffment in the eighth year of Tianshun. His nephew You Tan was established.
